question: Using the idea that a continuous function has a modulus of continuity that tends to zero as its argument tends to zero, explain why the sequence of Riemann sums \(\{S(f,X_n)\}\) associated to any sequence of tagged partitions \(\{X_n\}\) of \([a,b]\) with \(\|X_n\|\to 0\) is Cauchy.  In your explanation, explicitly use: (i) the fact that each \(X_n\) is a partition of \([a,b]\), (ii) the bound from theorem 2, and (iii) the definition of the modulus of continuity.
answer: Because each pair of successive partitions in the sequence can be viewed as a coarse and a fine partition, theorem 2 supplies a uniform Cauchy‑type estimate. Applying this estimate repeatedly and using that the modulus of continuity tends to zero as the norm tends to zero, the tail of the sequence of Riemann sums can be made arbitrarily small, proving that the sequence is Cauchy.

question: In the lecture it was shown that if \(f\) is a continuous function on \([a,b]\) and \(P\) and \(Q\) are two partitions with \(P\subset Q\), how do the limits of their Riemann sums relate to one another as the partitions become finer?
answer: Because \(P\subset Q\) (i.e., \(Q\) is finer than \(P\)), Theorem 2 guarantees that every Riemann sum over \(Q\) is squeezed between two Riemann sums over \(P\). As both partitions are made arbitrarily fine the two sets of sums converge to the same number, the integral of \(f\) on \([a,b]\).

question: The lecture described a simple trick to compare any two Riemann sums for arbitrary partitions. Explain how this trick uses partition refinement and the continuity of the function to establish comparability of the sums.
answer: The trick is to take two arbitrary partitions, say \(P\) and \(Q\), and form their common refinement \(P\\wedge Q\) (the partition consisting of all endpoints of both \(P\) and \(Q\)). Because each original partition is coarser than this refinement, Theorem 2 lets us compare the Riemann sums over \(P\), \(Q\), and \(P\\wedge Q\). The continuity of the function ensures the sums over the refinement converge, thereby allowing us to compare any two original sums.

Suppose a continuous function \(F\) is defined on the interval \([a,b]\) and that two tagged partitions \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) satisfy \(P_1\) finer than \(P_2\).  The lecture states that\n\[
|S(P_1,F)-S(P_2,F)|\le \omega_F(\|P_2\|)\,\lvert b-a\rvert .
\]\nFor a given tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), under what condition on \(\|P_2\|\) can we guarantee that the two Riemann sums differ by less than \(\varepsilon\)?  Explain why this follows from the behaviour of the modulus of continuity as its argument tends to zero.

Hence if \(\|P_2\|<\delta\) the desired inequality holds.

question: Let \(\{P_n\}\) be a sequence of tagged partitions of \([a,b]\) such that \(\|P_n\|\to 0\).  Using the bound above, show step‑by‑step why the corresponding sequence of Riemann sums \(\{S(P_n,F)\}\) is Cauchy.  In particular, explain how the norm of the coarser partition controls the difference of two terms of the sequence.
answer:
Choose \(m,n\) and let \(P_m\) be the coarser partition among \(P_m\) and \(P_n\).  By the lecture’s bound,
    \[
    |S(P_m,F)-S(P_n,F)|\le \omega_F(\|P_m\|)\,\lvert b-a\rvert .
    \]
    As \(\|P_m\|\to 0\) when \(m\to\infty\), the right‑hand side tends to zero.  Thus for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(N\) such that \(m,n\ge N\) implies \(|S(P_m,F)-S(P_n,F)|<\varepsilon\).  This is precisely the Cauchy criterion for \(\{S(P_n,F)\}\).

question: Let \(\{\,\mathcal{P}_r\,\}_{r\in\mathbb{N}}\) be a sequence of tagged partitions of \([a,b]\) with \(\|\mathcal{P}_r\|\to0\) and let \(\{S(f,\mathcal{P}_r)\}_{r}\) be the associated Riemann sums for a continuous function \(f\). Using the bound from Question 1, show that \(\{S(f,\mathcal{P}_r)\}\) is a Cauchy sequence. Explain how the completeness of \(\mathbb{R}\) then ensures the existence of a limit \(I\), and why this limit is the same for any such choice of partitions.
answer:
From Question 1 we have for any \(r,r'\) with sufficiently large \(r,r'\) (so that \(\|\mathcal{P}_r\|,\|\mathcal{P}_{r'}\|<\delta\)):\n\[\bigl|S(f,\mathcal{P}_r)-S(f,\mathcal{P}_{r'})\bigr|\le 2(b-a)\,\omega_f(\delta).\]  
Since \(\omega_f(\delta)\) can be made arbitrarily small by choosing \(\delta>0\) small, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(M\) such that for all \(r,r'\ge M\) the above difference is \(<\varepsilon\). That is exactly the Cauchy property. The real numbers form a complete metric space; therefore every Cauchy sequence in \(\mathbb{R}\) converges to a unique limit. Hence \(\{S(f,\mathcal{P}_r)\}\) converges to some \(I\in\mathbb{R}\). The same argument holds for any other sequence of partitions with vanishing norm, and the triangle‑inequality estimates ensure that the limits of all such sequences agree, so \(I\) is independent of the chosen sequence.

question: Assume that \(I\) is defined as the limit of one particular Cauchy sequence of Riemann sums \(\{S(f,\mathcal{P}_r)\}\). For an arbitrary sequence of tagged partitions \(\{\,\mathcal{Q}_s\,\}\) with \(\|\mathcal{Q}_s\|\to0\), outline how the triangle inequality and the squeeze theorem, together with the modulus of continuity bound, demonstrate that \(\lim_{s\to\infty}S(f,\mathcal{Q}_s)=I\). Which specific inequalities provide the upper and lower bounds in the squeeze argument?
answer:
Fix \(s\) and let \(\mathcal{Q}_s\) be a tagged partition with \(\|\mathcal{Q}_s\|\) small. Take the common refinement \(\mathcal{R}_s\) of \(\mathcal{Q}_s\) with the fixed partition sequence \(\mathcal{P}_r\) used to define \(I\). Then by the triangle inequality\n\[\bigl|S(f,\mathcal{Q}_s)-I\bigr|
 \le \bigl|S(f,\mathcal{Q}_s)-S(f,\mathcal{R}_s)\bigr|
   +\bigl|S(f,\mathcal{R}_s)-S(f,\mathcal{P}_r)\bigr|
   +\bigl|S(f,\mathcal{P}_r)-I\bigr|.\]  
Both the first and the second terms can be bounded by the modulus of continuity estimate: they are \(\le(b-a)\,\omega_f(\|\mathcal{Q}_s\|)\) and \(\le(b-a)\,\omega_f(\|\mathcal{P}_r\|)\) respectively. The third term is \(<\varepsilon/3\) once \(r\) is large, because \(\{S(f,\mathcal{P}_r)\}\) converges to \(I\). Thus we obtain\n\[\bigl|S(f,\mathcal{Q}_s)-I\bigr|
 \le (b-a)\,\omega_f(\|\mathcal{Q}_s\|)+(b-a)\,\omega_f(\|\mathcal{P}_r\|)+\varepsilon/3.\]  
With \(\|\mathcal{Q}_s\|\to0\) and \(\|\mathcal{P}_r\|\to0\), the right‑hand side tends to \(0\). This provides the two inequalities needed for the squeeze theorem—an upper bound tending to \(0\) and a trivial lower bound of \(-0\)—which forces the absolute difference to converge to zero. The modulus of continuity is the tool that turns the small mesh sizes of the partitions into a small difference of Riemann sums, enabling the squeeze argument.

Since the set never reaches \(\varepsilon\), we actually have \(\omega_f(\eta)<\varepsilon\).

question: For the linear function \(f(x)=ax+b\) the lecture states that the modulus of continuity is \(\omega_f(\eta)=|a|\eta\). Using this expression, explain how the uniform continuity of \(f\) on any closed and bounded interval follows, and specify how the \(\delta\) in the uniform‑continuity definition can be chosen in terms of \(\varepsilon\) and \(|a|\).
answer: Because \(|f(x)-f(y)|=|a||x-y|\), for every \(\eta>0\) the set \( \{\,|f(x)-f(y)| : |x-y|<\eta\,\}\) is bounded above by \(\sup(|a|\,|x-y|)=|a|\eta\). Thus \(\omega_f(\eta)=|a|\eta\). For uniform continuity, given any \(\varepsilon>0\) we choose \(\delta=\varepsilon/|a|\). Then \(|x-y|<\delta\) implies \(|f(x)-f(y)|=|a||x-y|<|a|\delta=\varepsilon\). Hence \(f\) is uniformly continuous on any closed, bounded interval, with \(\delta\) depending only on \(\varepsilon\) and the constant \(|a|\).

question: The professor showed that for every continuous function on a closed and bounded interval the modulus of continuity satisfies \(\lim_{\eta\to0}\omega_f(\eta)=0\), and that this fact is key to proving the existence of the Riemann integral. Explain the logical chain that links \(\omega_f(\eta)\to0\) with the fact that, as the mesh of a partition tends to \(0\), the corresponding Riemann sums converge to a single limit.
answer: The condition \(\lim_{\eta\to0}\omega_f(\eta)=0\) means that for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\eta_0>0\) such that whenever \(|x-y|<\eta_0\) we have \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon/(b-a)\). Take a tagged partition whose mesh (norm) is \(<\eta_0\). Then every subinterval has length \(<\eta_0\), so the oscillation of \(f\) on each subinterval is \(<\varepsilon/(b-a)\). The difference between the corresponding upper and lower sums is therefore bounded by \((b-a)\times\varepsilon/(b-a)=\varepsilon\). Thus as the partition mesh shrinks to \(0\), the upper and lower sums squeeze to a common limit—precisely the Riemann integral of \(f\).

answer: The set in question is the collection of all differences \(|f(x)-f(y)|\) for pairs with \(|x-y|<\eta\). By the uniform‑continuity part of the lecture, there is a \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-y|<\delta\) implies \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon/2\). Choosing \(\eta=\delta\) ensures that every element of the set is \(<\varepsilon/2\); hence \(\varepsilon/2\) is an upper bound of the set. By the upper‑bound theorem, the supremum of the set cannot exceed any upper bound, so \(\sup\{\,|f(x)-f(y)|:|x-y|<\eta\,\}\leq\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon\). Consequently \(\omega_f(\eta)\leq\varepsilon\), fulfilling the \(\varepsilon\)–\(\delta\) requirement in the proof.

question: In the lecture, a continuous function \(f\) on an interval \([a,b]\) is approximated by Riemann sums built from a tagged partition.  As the partitions get finer, the norm of each partition goes to zero.  Explain why the limit of these Riemann sums exists and equals the Riemann integral, and describe how this limit is represented geometrically in terms of the graph of \(f\).
answer: The limit of the Riemann sums exists because, as the norm of the partition tends to zero, the difference between successive Riemann sums becomes arbitrarily small for a continuous function.  This limit is defined as the Riemann integral \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\).  Geometrically, it equals the area bounded by the graph of \(f\), the \(x\)-axis, and the vertical lines at \(x=a\) and \(x=b\), since each Riemann sum approximates that area by a sum of rectangles whose heights are the function values at the tags.

question: During the discussion, it was noted that for any two sequences of tagged partitions \(\{P_k\}\) and \(\{Q_k\}\) over the same interval \([a,b]\) with \(\|P_k\|\to0\) and \(\|Q_k\|\to0\), the corresponding Riemann sums of a continuous function \(f\) converge to the same number.  Using the ideas presented, argue why the limits of the Riemann sums from the two sequences must coincide and why that common limit is defined to be the Riemann integral of \(f\).
answer: Because both sequences of partitions refine the interval so that the longest subinterval shrinks to zero, the variation of \(f\) over each subinterval becomes arbitrarily small.  Consequently, for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists a stage beyond which all Riemann sums from both sequences differ from each other by less than \(\varepsilon\).  Hence the two limits are equal, and this common value is by definition the Riemann integral of \(f\) over \([a,b]\).

question: The lecture described a linearity property: the Riemann sum of the sum of two functions equals the sum of their individual Riemann sums for any fixed tagged partition.  Write this property in LaTeX, then explain how it leads to the statement that \(\displaystyle \int_a^b (f+g)\,dx = \int_a^b f\,dx + \int_a^b g\,dx\).
answer:
For a tagged partition \((P,\tau)\) we have  
    \[
      S(f+g,P,\tau)=\sum_{i=1}^n (f+g)(\tau_i)\,\Delta x_i
      =\sum_{i=1}^n f(\tau_i)\,\Delta x_i+\sum_{i=1}^n g(\tau_i)\,\Delta x_i
      =S(f,P,\tau)+S(g,P,\tau).
    \]  
    Taking the limit as the norm of \(P\) tends to zero gives  
    \[
      \int_a^b (f+g)(x)\,dx = \lim_{\|P\|\to0}S(f+g,P,\tau)
      = \lim_{\|P\|\to0}S(f,P,\tau)+\lim_{\|P\|\to0}S(g,P,\tau)
      = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx + \int_a^b g(x)\,dx.
    \]

How does this property guarantee the existence of the Riemann integral of \(F\) according to the lecture?
answer: The modulus of continuity says that for any small \(\eta\) the oscillation of \(F\) over intervals of length at most \(\eta\) is bounded by \(\omega(\eta)\), which becomes arbitrarily small when \(\eta\) does. When partitions have norm less than \(\eta\), the difference between the supremum and infimum of \(F\) on each subinterval is at most \(\omega(\eta)\); hence all Riemann sums for such partitions lie within a band of width at most \((b-a)\omega(\eta)\). As \(\eta\to0\) that band collapses to a single value, which proves that the Riemann sums converge to a unique limit. Thus the continuity (via the vanishing modulus) guarantees existence of the integral.

question: The notes state that the Riemann sum of a sum of functions equals the sum of the Riemann sums, and that the limit of a sum of limits equals the sum of limits.  Using this fact, explain how one deduces the linearity property of the Riemann integral from the properties of Riemann sums.
answer:
For two functions \(F\) and \(G\) and a given partition, the Riemann sum satisfies  
\[
S(F+G)=S(F)+S(G).
\]
Taking limits over any sequence whose norm \(\to 0\) gives  
\[
\lim S(F+G)=\lim S(F)+\lim S(G).
\]
Since the limits on the right are precisely the Riemann integrals \(\int F\) and \(\int G\), we obtain  
\[
\int (F+G)=\int F+\int G,
\]
which is the linearity property of the integral.

question: In the lecture, it was shown that the limit of the Riemann sums exists for every sequence of partitions of \([a,b]\) whose norm tends to zero.  Explain why two different real numbers cannot both serve as such limits, and how this argument establishes the uniqueness of the Riemann integral.
answer: Two different real numbers cannot both arise as limits because the limit of a convergent sequence of real numbers is unique.  In the lecture we consider arbitrary sequences of partitions with norm → 0; for each such sequence the Riemann sums \(S(F,P_n)\) converge to *some* real number.  If there were two distinct numbers, say \(L_1\) and \(L_2\), that could be obtained as limits from different sequences, then we would have two convergent sequences of Riemann sums approaching different limits – a contradiction to the uniqueness of limits.  Therefore a single real number serves as the limit for all such sequences, which is precisely the definition of the Riemann integral, establishing its uniqueness.

The lecture demonstrates that for any partition \(P\) of \([a,b]\) we have the algebraic identity  
    \[
    S(F+G,P)=S(F,P)+S(G,P).

    \[
    \int_a^b (F+G)\,dx=\int_a^b F\,dx+\int_a^b G\,dx,
    \]

question: The notes mention the modulus of continuity of a continuous function \(f\) and state that it tends to \(0\) as the interval length \(\eta\) tends to \(0\). Using this fact, explain why every sequence of partitions of \([a,b]\) whose norm approaches \(0\) yields Riemann sums that converge to the same number, i.e. why \(\int_a^b f\,dx\) is well‑defined for continuous \(f\).
answer: For a continuous \(f\), the modulus of continuity \(\omega(\eta)=\sup_{|x-y|\le\eta}|f(x)-f(y)|\) satisfies \(\omega(\eta)\to0\) as \(\eta\to0\). Hence, when the norm of a partition \(P\) is \(\le\eta\), any two points within the same subinterval differ by at most \(\eta\), making the contribution of any two sampled points within that subinterval differ by no more than \(\omega(\eta)\). Summing over all subintervals shows that all Riemann sums for partitions of norm \(\le\eta\) lie within \((b-a)\,\omega(\eta)\) of each other. As \(\eta\to0\), this bound goes to \(0\), forcing all such sums to converge to the same limit. Therefore the integral \(\int_a^b f\,dx\) is uniquely defined for continuous \(f\).

question: The lecture states that for continuous functions \(f\) and \(g\) on \([a,b]\) and a real number \(\alpha\), the Riemann integral satisfies a linearity rule.  State this rule and explain the reasoning that leads from the continuity of \(f\) and \(g\) to the equality \(\displaystyle \int_{a}^{b}(\alpha f+g)\,dx=\alpha\int_{a}^{b}f\,dx+\int_{a}^{b}g\,dx\).
answer:
The linearity rule is \[
    \int_{a}^{b}(\alpha f+g)\,dx=\alpha\int_{a}^{b}f\,dx+\int_{a}^{b}g\,dx\,.
    \]  Since \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous on \([a,b]\), each is Riemann‑integrable.  The Riemann sum for \(\alpha f+g\) splits additively into the sum for \(\alpha f\) and the sum for \(g\); scaling by \(\alpha\) pulls out of the integral, and the additivity of limits gives the stated equality.
